content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies privacy leakage by attacking gradients in federated learning. The authors proposed using dataset condensation to mitigate such risks, which however introduced trade-off between accuracy, privacy, and time complexity. Experiments on some small datasets and models demonstrate the effect of privacy protection by using dataset condensation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
* The authors revealed that though dataset condensation can degrade data reconstruction compared to FedAvg, the large overhead could be an obstacle for resource-limited devices, like NVIDIA Jeston.
* The authors both qualitatively and visually analyze the privacy advantage of using condensed dataset in place of original data.
* Different types of trade-off have been intensively studed on different datasets, including privacy-accuracy and accuracy-time.

Weakness:
* The major challenges of the paper should be on the attack on reconstructing data from gradients but they are not sufficiently explained in the introduction. The introduction for the gradient attacks is too concise in the the first paragraph of page 2. The authors should elaborate on when and how the gradients can be used to reconstruct the data. Only on the sucessful cases of the attacks, the work can be motivated.
* The technical contribution is marginal compared to the distilled one-shot federated learning [A]. Previously, the privacy advantage of dataset condensation (CD) has been previously demonstrated [B].
* The evaluated models are too small for effective gradient attacks. Successful gradient attacks (Geiping, et al., 2020) relies on a overparameterized models, like wide ResNet18 to Resnet50 on CIFAR10. Evaluation on small models like MLP, LeNet, can not sufficiently demonstrate the strength of the defenses.

[A] Zhou, Yanlin, George Pu, Xiyao Ma, Xiaolin Li, and Dapeng Wu. "Distilled one-shot federated learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2009.07999 (2020).

[B] Dong, T., Zhao, B., & Lyu, L. (2022). Privacy for Free: How does Dataset Condensation Help Privacy?. ICML.


Minor issues:
* Citations should be (Name, et al., 2020) instead of Name et al., 2020 in many places.
* In the last pargraph of Introduction, the abbrevation, DOSFL+, is introduced before definition.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper should be proofread and polished before submission. For example, the introduction mostly focus on the federated learning framework but not the major challenges. 

Quality: The evaluation is insufficient to demonstrate the effectiveness of defense when large models are used in FL.

Novelty: Since the privacy advantage of dataset condensation (CD) has been previously demonstrated and analyzed by [B], the novelty could be marginal as applying CD in federated learning.

Reproducibility is okay as the dataset condensation (CD) itself has been an open-sourced technique. Plugging CD into the federated learning may not cause technical challenges.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studied how dataset condensation improves privacy protection in federated learning. Though I appreciate the empirical contributions that demonstrate the use case of dataset condensation, the novelty is marginal compared to previous works [A, B]. The empirical evaluation is not solid enough to support the claim that the dataset condensation is a strong tool for privacy protection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Federated learning shares the gradient updates trained from local private data and previous work shows that it is possible that local data is leaked by gradient. This paper proposes to use synthesized data for federated learning to defend the gradient recovering attack.This paper proposes to use existing data condensation method DCGM to synthesize data. The evaluation shows that the proposed method can reduce the reconstruction of gradient based attacks but also suffers accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
+ The idea of training on synthesized data to improve the privacy of the federated learning is interesting.

Cons:
-  My major concern is that the proposed approach seems too simple and the performance is not good. This paper seems to just apply an existing dataset condensation method (DCGM) in federated learning. The proposed method also has 20% accuracy degradation in CIFAR10 which make this method much less valuable. 

- The improvement over existing method DOSFL+ seems little. Table 2 shows similar accuracy between the proposed method and DOSFL+. Figure 3 and 4 show the recovered images look similar between the proposed method and DOSFL+. I do not see the improvement of the proposed method over the existing method. 

- Need to evaluate new attacks to see if the proposed defense can survive new attacks such as [1].

- Misc.
In abstract, the client’s then train… should be the client then train…

[1] Hatamizadeh, A., Yin, H., Molchanov, P., Myronenko, A., Li, W., Dogra, P., ... & Roth, H. (2021). Towards Understanding the Risks of Gradient Inversion in Federated Learning.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is clear to read. The novelty is limited. I do not know if the details privided.in this paper is enough for reproducing its experiment's result.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the limited novelty and weak performance, I recommend rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes use dataset condensation as a privacy enhancing tool for federated learning. The authors propose to generate synthetic data following the DCGM method by Zhao et al. 2022 and utilize the synthetic data for FL training. The proposed method is harder for existing attack method to reconstruct the training images compared to non private baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- This work explores how to use synthetic data to enhance privacy in federated learning, which itself is an interesting area to explore.
- Empirical results have shown that the proposed method achieves larger reconstruction error compared to baseline methods.
Weakness:
- The novelty of this work is limited. The method is a simple combination of DCGM and FedAvg. It doesn't seem to me what are the challenges to apply DCGM in federated setting. Could the authors justify what is new in this work?
- It is misleading to say DCGM protects privacy for federated learning. Without defining what privacy information is, it is hard to argue what the proposed method is protecting. From the empirical results, it only seems that using synthetic data helps increasing the reconstruction error, where the error is defined as MSE between the reconstructed image and the true training image. However, it is improper to translate this MSE metric to privacy (for example, the MSE between a rotated image and the true image is huge but obviously there isn't any information loss from rotating the image). Therefore, it is not convincing to me that the proposed method is private.
- It also seems that on CIFAR 10, the utility drops significantly when trained on synthetic data. Given that there's no formal privacy guarantee, I'm wondering how effective the method itself is. Could the authors provide a curve between size of synthetic data and utility on CIFAR 10?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Novelty is limited. Motivations and formal justification needs to be improved.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors combine DCGM with FedAvg to protect against gradient inversion attacks. However, the authors fail to make a justification on the privacy side of the proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed to enhance privacy in federated learning (FL) by using dataset condensation. The main idea is that each client in FL uses some dataset condensation technique to independently construct a smaller condensed dataset from their own sensitive data. This condensed data is then used as normal in FL. The authors empirically show that the chosen gradient reconstruction attacks do not work as well on the condensed dataset, as with the baselines (no privacy protection or send the condensed dataset to the server as is). The tests use standard datasets and models (LeNet+MNIST, ConvNet+CIFAR10, simple MLP+Fashion MNIST).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

1) The topic of protecting privacy in FL is important.


### Weaknesses:

The following are the major issues I have with the paper, combined with some questions for the authors.

#### Major problems:


1) The paper completely ignores existing methods and theory for privacy protection. Specifically, differential privacy (DP, Dwork et al 2006, see Dwork and Roth 2014 for an introduction) is the go-to privacy definition that needs to be discussed on some level in (almost) any machine learning paper that aims for privacy protection. There are well-established DP techniques for protecting gradients (e.g. DP stochastic gradient descent, see Song et al. 2013).

2) Related to previous point, for measuring attack success, you should also consider membership inference attacks: this requires the attacker to simply guess a single bit correctly, and if this is not succesful, more complicated tasks like reconstructions will not work either (see e.g. Carlini et al. 2021).

3) The paper also fails to mention Dong et al. 2022, which also proposes to use dataset condensation for protecting privacy (but see Carlini et al. 2022 for a discussion on what is wrong in that paper). 

4) Zhu et al. 2019 already noted that, e.g., gradient compression techniques can mitigate gradient reconstruction attacks. If you simply aim to protect from the reconstructions, you should note this and compare to the state-of-the-art in these as well.

5) How did you choose the hyperparameters in the experiments? And especially, how did you choose the batch sizes, and why are different methods using differing batch sizes?


#### Minor problems:

i) The paper seems very rushed (e.g. check citations: cite vs citep etc.).

ii) Some notations seem very confusing: e.g. D_i is true data and tilde D_i is condensed, while tilde w are the model weights trained on true data, w weights trained on condensed data, and x,y are samples from the condensed data.

iii) There seems to be some confusion on whether the clients communicate gradients or trained model weights (see e.g. p.4 second last paragraph before Sec.4). Please clarify this.

iv) p.1: "In the FL framework, clients independently train their models", the training is clearly not independent. Please clarify.

v) p.8: "In the case of MNIST we can see that the condensed images carry the natural image prior". What prior are you talking about, what does this mean?

vi) Fig.6: Lenet should be MNIST maybe?


#### References

Carlini et al. 2021: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles.

Carlini et al. 2022: No Free Lunch in "Privacy for Free: How does Dataset Condensation Help Privacy".

Dong et al. 2022: Privacy for Free: How does Dataset Condensation Help Privacy?

Dwork et al. 2006: Calibrating noise to sensitivity in private data analysis.

Dwork and Roth 2014: Algorithmic foundations of DP.

Song et al. 2013: Stochastic gradient descent with DP updates.

Zhu et al. 2019: Deep leakage from gradients.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is often sloppy and seems rushed (plenty of typos, bad citation technique, some unintentional seeming repetitions etc.). The proposed approach is not really novel, and the paper fails to discuss any existing methods and theory. Hyperparameter values seem to be listed, so it might be possible reproduce the key findings from this paper. There does not seem to be any code available.
content.summary_of_the_review: A rushed-feeling paper with several major problems. Clearly not ready for publication.

content.title: ENHANCING THE PRIVACY OF FEDERATED LEARNING THROUGH DATA SYNTHESIS
content.abstract:
Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning architecture where edge devices collaboratively learn the shared model, while the training data is securely held at the edge devices. FL promises a way forward to preserving data privacy by sending model updates in the form of gradients or the weights themselves. However, these updates still contain the essence of the original training data and can be
reconstructed using gradient-based attacks. To overcome this, we propose a novel Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning algorithm (PPFed) wherein we generate a condensed dataset from the original training data at each edge device. The client’s then train their local models on the condensed dataset which is then broadcasted to the server, followed by regular federated averaging. Our method provides privacy by being robust against gradient-based attacks, which holds across different benchmark datasets and CNN based architectures
